title: How To Get Every Student To Participate
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Opening with an anecdote about William James lying down in class when student participation waned, Linsin lays out the "index card method" as a concrete fix for uneven classroom participation. The technique is simple: write each student's name on an individual index card, shuffle the deck, and cold-call the name on top after every question, marking the date on the back of the card to track participation. His central claim is that random, unavoidable cold-calling — rather than relying on volunteers — is what actually gets every student intellectually engaged rather than letting a vocal few dominate discussion. He notes practical variations, such as reshuffling after each question so students can be called on repeatedly, and quietly previewing the deck when a teacher wants to ensure certain students get called. Beyond simply increasing participation, he argues the method compounds over time: students grow more comfortable voicing ideas, begin challenging each other's thinking, and discussions deepen as self-consciousness fades. The piece closes by insisting participation shouldn't be treated as optional — it should be taught, expected, and graded like any other skill.
points: The index card method: name cards, reshuffled after every question, with the top card cold-called and dated on the back.
Random unavoidable cold-calling is credited with keeping all students "perpetually on their toes," not just the vocal few.
Teachers can quietly preview the shuffled deck if they want to make sure specific students get called that day.
Over time the method is said to make students more comfortable voicing opinions and more willing to challenge each other's ideas.
quotes: 19th Century psychologist and Harvard professor William James believed so strongly that teaching was a mutual process that when his students’ participation waned he would lie down in class as if to take a nap.
So how do you get everyone involved? Luckily, there is a surefire method. It’s also easy and has the added benefit of keeping them wide awake.
I recommend a quick shuffle after every question. This way, a student could potentially be called on again, thereby keeping them perpetually on their toes.
Great teachers don’t let students hide. Participation isn’t a choice. No excuses.
In this classroom, you will be called on so you better be ready for it.
